notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes based on the sources available. I indicate clearly what each source says and where I couldn't find material from a particular tradition.

---

## Luke 10:22-42 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 22: *"All things have been entrusted to Me by My Father. No one knows who the Son is except the Father, and no one knows who the Father is except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him."*

**Traditional Reading (shared broadly across Protestantism):**

- **Ellicott** notes that "All things" refers specially to the mysteries of the kingdom implied in the word "reveal" — the wider meaning appears in Matthew 28:18. The "knowing" here means full, complete, intimate knowledge. No one can fully comprehend the Son except the Father, and no one fully enters into the Fatherhood of God except the Son. Only through Christ is the Father revealed. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm
- **David Guzik (Enduring Word)** says Jesus spoke here of His unity with the Father ("All things have been delivered to Me"), His special relationship with the Father (mutual exclusive knowledge), and how God allows believers to share in that relationship ("the one to whom the Son wills to reveal Him"). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/
- **Matthew 11:27 Commentaries (biblehub.com)** explains: "No man knoweth the Son — that is, such is the nature of the Son of God, such the mystery of the union between the divine and human nature, such his exalted character as 'divine,' that no mortal can fully comprehend Jesus. None but God fully knows him." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/11-27.htm

**Reformed / Baptist Perspective:**

- **DesiringGod.org (John Piper)** stresses that Jesus knows the Father "the way an omniscient Person knows himself." Our knowledge of the Father depends wholly on Jesus' gracious revelation; it is "derivative and partial and imperfect." The Son's revelation is inseparable from the gospel invitation: "Come to me, all who labor…" (Matt 11:28, immediately following). The eternal Son-Father relationship precedes creation. — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/god-in-skin-and-time ; https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/in-him-are-hid-all-the-treasures-of-wisdom-and-knowledge

**Lutheran Perspective:**

- **1517.org** frames this verse within the Reformation teaching of *Deus absconditus* (the hidden God) vs. *Deus revelatus* (the revealed God). Jesus praises the Father for hiding things, then shifts to speaking *as* the revealed God. We cannot know God apart from God's gracious self-disclosure; God is hidden — and that can be terrifying. But Jesus draws our attention from the hidden God to Himself as the revealed God who saves, culminating at the cross. — https://www.1517.org/articles/gospel-matthew-1125-30-reformation-sunday-series-c

**Catholic / Orthodox:** No specific material found on this verse from the approved Catholic/Orthodox sites.

---

### vv. 23-24: *"Then Jesus turned to the disciples and said privately, 'Blessed are the eyes that see what you see…'"*

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Ellicott** notes this is another instance of repeated words — Matthew reports them as spoken after the parable of the Sower (Matt 13:16). Luke's version has "prophets and kings" instead of Matthew's "prophets and righteous men." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)** does not expand substantially on these verses beyond noting the privilege of the disciples in seeing what prophets and kings longed to see. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/

**Denominational differences:** No distinctive tradition-specific material found for these two verses.

---

### v. 25: *An expert in the law stood up to test Him: "Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?"*

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Ellicott** says the word "tempting" does not necessarily imply hostile purpose — it was a test-question to see if the new Teacher was sound on the ethical obligations of the Law. Unlike the rich young ruler (Matt 19), this questioner has "a certain tone of self-conscious superiority." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm
- **David Guzik (Enduring Word)** notes the Greek word for "tested" isn't necessarily mean or evil — it may have been a sincere question from a sincere seeker. He also notes that "eternal life" in the biblical sense refers to a quality of life from God that we can have right now, not merely duration. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/
- **bible.org** emphasizes that the lawyer's question implies he expected one decisive act, not a sequence. Jesus does not answer directly but asks him what the Law says, retaining His authority. — https://bible.org/seriespage/good-samaritan-luke-1025-37

**Bridgeway Bible Commentary:** The lawyer thought of eternal life as something obtained by some special act. Jesus showed it is "inseparably linked with the way people live their daily lives." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/luke-10.html

---

### v. 26: *"What is written in the Law? How do you read it?"*

- **Ellicott:** "As the method of Socrates was to make men conscious of their ignorance of the true meaning of words which they repeated glibly, so here our Lord parries the question by another." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm
- **bible.org:** Jesus restrains Himself from giving an answer and instead says, "You know the law, how does it read to you?" He treats the lawyer as the student and Himself as the Teacher. — https://bible.org/seriespage/good-samaritan-luke-1025-37

---

### v. 27: *"'Love the Lord your God with all your heart…' and 'Love your neighbor as yourself.'"*

- **bible.org:** The answer the lawyer gives is "absolutely correct" and identical with the answer our Lord gave when asked a similar question. There is no difference of opinion about the essence of the law. — https://bible.org/seriespage/good-samaritan-luke-1025-37

---

### v. 28: *"You have answered correctly. Do this and you will live."*

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Ellicott:** Jesus' acceptance of the lawyer's answer as theoretically true was part of His teaching method. "This do, and thou shalt live" were words "of a Prophet who knew what was in the man, and read the secrets of his heart, and saw how little love was to be found there." Yet Jesus does more than accommodate the legal viewpoint: "Love was really life, at once its source and its manifestation, if only the love were true, and the test of its being true was action." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm

**Evangelical (bible.org):** This is a crucial point: Jesus is NOT teaching works as a means of salvation. He is actually teaching that doing good works (law-keeping) cannot save anyone, because no one can keep the law perfectly. "Jesus sought to show this self-confident lawyer that by his own definitions, law keeping was not the pathway to eternal life, because no one is able to live up to the demands of the law." The law can only condemn, not save. — https://bible.org/seriespage/good-samaritan-luke-1025-37

---

### v. 29: *"But wanting to justify himself, he asked Jesus, 'And who is my neighbor?'"*

- **Ellicott:** "The question implied a conscience half-awakened and uneasy. It is characteristic that no doubt seems to cross his mind as to his love of God. There he felt that he was safe." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm
- **Adam Clarke:** The lawyer was "wishing to make it appear that he was a righteous man." He supposed the answer would be "Every Jew" — and he imagined he had never been deficient toward any Jew. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/luke-10.html
- **bible.org:** The lawyer begins "to do what some lawyers do so well — look for a technicality in the law itself." He's uneasy about the command to love his neighbor because he knows his love is deficient. — https://bible.org/seriespage/good-samaritan-luke-1025-37

---

### v. 30: *"A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho when he fell into the hands of robbers…"*

- **Ellicott:** The journey was about 21 miles through rocky, desert country with caves haunted by robbers. In Jerome's time it was known as the "red" or "bloody" way. Ellicott suggests the parable may be an actual history that Jesus observed. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm
- **ICC (International Critical Commentary):** "We may believe that the narrative is not fiction, but history. Jesus would not be likely to invent such behaviour, and attribute it to priest, Levite, and Samaritan, if it had not actually occurred." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/icc/luke-10.html
- **bible.org:** Note that the racial origins of the victim are deliberately not stated. "The reason is simple — it doesn't matter." The only thing that matters is that he is badly hurt and in need of help. — https://bible.org/seriespage/good-samaritan-luke-1025-37

---

### vv. 31-32: *The priest and the Levite pass by on the other side.*

- **Ellicott:** Jericho was a priestly city, so a priest returning from his week of Temple service has a touch of "vivid naturalness." The priest may have shrunk from trouble and peril, and from fear of ceremonial defilement from contact with a possible corpse. The Levite is "at once better and worse than the priest — better in that he does not altogether turn aside, but 'comes' and looks; worse in that his second thoughts are at variance with his first." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm
- **bible.org:** The priest "deliberately walked on the other side of the road, so as not to get too close." He did not check if the man was alive or dead. "For this priest, ignorance was indeed bliss." The Levite's actions were "a virtual re-play." Both show revulsion, not compassion. — https://bible.org/seriespage/good-samaritan-luke-1025-37

---

### v. 33: *"But when a Samaritan on a journey came upon him, he looked at him and had compassion."*

- **Ellicott:** Notes the change of word — it was not likely the hated alien would be coming down from Jerusalem. His journey would probably be to or from Bethel and Gerizim. "Here there is a true human feeling in one who outwardly was involved in heresy and schism, and our Lord singles that out as infinitely preferable to the form of godliness without its power." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm
- **bible.org:** The Samaritan, unlike the priest and Levite, "has a reason for his journey. He is on a trip. If anyone could excuse himself from getting involved, it was this Samaritan." Yet he felt compassion — the critical difference. — https://bible.org/seriespage/good-samaritan-luke-1025-37

---

### v. 34: *"He went to him and bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine…"*

- **Ellicott:** "All fear of risk from robbers, or from the police of Rome, who might take him for a robber, is put aside; the 'oil and wine,' which had been provided for personal refreshment, are freely given." The wine was for cleansing wounds, the oil for soothing inflammation. The Samaritan gave up his own animal and walked. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm
- **David Guzik (Enduring Word):** "The wine, containing alcohol, had an antiseptic effect on the man's wounds. The oil helped to soothe the wounds, easing the pain. To set him on his own animal meant that the Samaritan himself walked." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/

---

### v. 35: *Two denarii given to the innkeeper.*

- **Ellicott:** Two denarii was the average wages of a labourer for two days (Matt 20:2), or enough for a meal for 25 men (Mark 6:37). "It was therefore a sufficient and liberal provision for all probable contingencies." The Samaritan also gave a "carte blanche for whatever else might be required." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm

---

### vv. 36-37: *"Which of these three do you think was a neighbor…" "The one who showed him mercy." "Go and do likewise."*

- **Ellicott:** "This was the practical, though not the formal, answer to the question of the lawyer. If he acted in the spirit of the Samaritan, he would need no 'nicely-calculated less or more' of casuistic distinctions as to who was and who was not his neighbour." The problem is solved by loving: *Solvitur amando.* — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm
- **Adam Clarke:** The lawyer's "prejudice would not permit him to name the Samaritan, yet his conscience obliged him to acknowledge that he was the only righteous person of the three." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/luke-10.html
- **David Guzik (Enduring Word):** "Jesus allowed the parable to answer the lawyer's question and guide the application. I am to love my neighbor, and my neighbor is the one who others might consider my enemy. My neighbor is the one with a need right in front of me." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/
- **bible.org:** "The lawyer really chokes on his words here. He cannot find it in himself to even pronounce the word 'Samaritan,' and so he answers, 'The one who showed mercy toward him.'" Jesus twice tells this man to "do" — not because works save, but because this man must first see the bankruptcy of his law-keeping system before he can turn to Christ. — https://bible.org/seriespage/good-samaritan-luke-1025-37

**1517.org (Lutheran) notes** that Luke places the Mary and Martha story "immediately on the heels of the Parable of the Good Samaritan. At the end of that teaching, Jesus was clear, serving those who are in need is neither optional nor unimportant. So, we should not read Jesus as saying one thing in verse 37 and the opposite in verse 42." — https://www.1517.org/articles/gospel-luke-1038-42-pentecost-6-series-c-2025

---

### v. 38: *"As they traveled along, Jesus entered a village where a woman named Martha welcomed Him into her home."*

- **Ellicott:** The village was almost certainly Bethany (cf. John 11:1). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm
- **Adam Clarke:** "If this village was Bethany, where Martha and Mary lived, [it was] at less than two miles' distance from Jerusalem." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/luke-10.html
- **bible.org:** Based on all the texts, Martha appears to be the older sister — the hostess, more aggressive and outspoken. — https://bible.org/seriespage/when-martha-was-mad-master-luke-1038-42
- **1517.org (Lutheran):** Emphasizes the personal nature: "Martha is not a category or a type of person, she is a woman with a name who welcomed our Lord into her home." These are real women, not archetypes. — https://www.1517.org/articles/gospel-luke-1038-42-pentecost-6-series-c-2

---

### v. 39: *"She had a sister named Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet listening to His message."*

- **Ellicott:** The imperfect tense ἤκουεν indicates "she continued to listen." The meal had not yet begun; Mary was sitting at His feet "as His disciple" (cf. Acts 22:3). Ellicott notes the identity of character here matches the accounts in John 11 and 12. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm
- **bible.org:** Mary was always at Jesus' feet — in every text that mentions her (Luke 7, Luke 10, John 11, John 12). The author suggests she initially went to wash Jesus' feet (as a good hostess would) and "just never got up" because she was captivated by His words. — https://bible.org/seriespage/when-martha-was-mad-master-luke-1038-42
- **ICC:** "The meal has not yet begun, for Martha is preparing it; and Mary is not sitting at table with Him, but at His feet as His disciple." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/icc/luke-10.html
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** Mary sat "in rapt attention, submissive and obedient" as a disciple and learner. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/luke-10.html

---

### v. 40: *"But Martha was distracted by all the preparations to be made…"*

- **Ellicott:** The Greek for "cumbered" (KJV) is literally "was distracted" — drawn hither and thither by conflicting cares. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm
- **bible.org:** Martha accuses both Mary and Jesus of wrongdoing, charges Jesus with not caring, condoning wrongdoing, and publicly demands Jesus concede His "error." Martha was not envious of Mary but angry with her — she felt working in the kitchen was the "better thing" for both of them. "Martha had a serving ministry, but not a servant's heart." — https://bible.org/seriespage/when-martha-was-mad-master-luke-1038-42
- **ICC (textual note):** The Greek word περιεσπᾶτο is used only once in the NT — BDAG says it could mean "quite busy" or "overburdened." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/icc/luke-10.html

---

### vv. 41-42: *"Martha, Martha… you are worried and upset about many things. But only one thing is necessary…"*

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Ellicott:** The repetition of the name "conveys an expression of affection and concern" (cf. Luke 22:31; Acts 9:4). The verb μεριμνᾷς is "a strong one, 'thou art anxious,' and implies division and distraction of mind (μερίζω), which believers ought to avoid" (cf. Matt 6:25; Phil 4:6; 1 Pet 5:7). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm
- **Ellicott** notes a textual variant: some better MSS read "There is need of few things, or of one only." This could be taken literally (we need only a single dish) or spiritually (the one thing needed is devout, intent love). "It is not improbable that our Lord designedly used words which had an outer and an inner meaning." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm
- **Spurgeon (quoted in Enduring Word):** "The one thing needful evidently is that which Mary chose — that good part which should not be taken away from her. Very clearly this was to sit at Jesus' feet, and hear his word." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/
- **David Guzik:** "Mary's good part was her simple devotion to Jesus, loving Him by listening to His word." Jesus was not condemning Martha's service — but she had not added the one thing needed. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-10/
- **Ellicott** on "that good part": The Greek noun is nearly the same as what the younger son uses in Luke 15:12 for "the portion of goods" — the good portion here being nothing less than eternal life. There is "something approaching to a half-playful mingling of the higher and lower meanings of the word." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/10.htm

**Reformed Perspective:**

- **R.C. Sproul (Ligonier):** "Notice that Jesus did not say, 'Martha, Mary has chosen the good part, and you've chosen the bad part.' Jesus was not saying that serving the way Martha had been serving was a bad thing to do. This was not a contrast, but a comparative analysis." Serving was a good thing; the better thing was attending to Jesus' teaching. — https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/martha-mary

**Lutheran Perspective:**

- **1517.org:** Jesus does not criticize Martha for serving. He does not scold her at all. Luke describes her as "distracted" (περιεσπᾶτο) — possibly just "quite busy." Jesus simply names her feelings and "His only word to her is about the goodness of what Mary is doing. He seems to be saying to Martha that, while her serving is worthwhile, Mary is doing something even better." The better option is listening to Jesus. Also, the placement after the Good Samaritan is intentional: "It seems Mary and Martha each focused on one of" the two great commandments — Mary on loving God, Martha on loving neighbor. "Rather than pitting service against study or love of God against love of the neighbor, perhaps the problem in this text is not so much Martha's misplaced priorities as it is that each of us is finite. We are incapable of doing everything at once." — https://www.1517.org/articles/gospel-luke-1038-42-pentecost-6-series-c-2 ; https://www.1517.org/articles/gospel-luke-1038-42-pentecost-6-series-c-2025

**Evangelical (bible.org):** Jesus' response reveals several things: (1) He responded without anger — His rebuke was most gentle. (2) He refused to impose a stereotypical "woman's role" on Mary and Martha — Mary was commended for sitting and learning. (3) Jesus dealt more with attitudes than actions — Martha was rebuked for being "worried and upset," not for serving. (4) Martha's problem was priorities — the "better thing" was "abiding in Christ, drawing strength and instruction from Him." (5) Martha had overstepped her responsibilities — she felt responsible for Mary's ministry and even to dictate Jesus' responsibilities. — https://bible.org/seriespage/when-martha-was-mad-master-luke-1038-42

**Modern Scholarship:**

- **Bible Odyssey** notes a less conventional reading: "Martha is not shown doing housework, and Jesus doesn't specify what the 'one thing…the better part' is. Rather, Martha is a householder who hosts Jesus; she is engaged in much 'work' or, better, 'service' (Greek: *diakonian*). By contrast, Luke depicts Mary as a disciple sitting at Jesus' feet. Both women are engaged in different aspects of ministry." Mary Stromer Hanson observes "it isn't even clear that Mary is in the house with Martha and Jesus; possibly, Martha's complaint is that Mary's discipleship has taken her away from home." — https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/mary-and-martha/

**Catholic / Orthodox:** No specific material found from the approved Catholic/Orthodox sites for this passage.

**Prosperity / Word of Faith / Hyper-Grace:** No specific material found from the approved sites addressing these traditions on this passage.

---

## Summary of Where Protestant Traditions Differ

| Passage | Nature of Difference |
|---|---|
| **v. 22** | Lutheran (1517.org) frames it uniquely through Luther's categories of *Deus absconditus / revelatus* — the terror of the hidden God resolved only in Christ revealed. Reformed (DesiringGod) stresses the eternal, intra-Trinitarian knowing as the basis of our adoption. |
| **vv. 25-28** | Evangelical (bible.org) strongly emphasizes that Jesus is *not* teaching salvation by works but exposing the impossibility of law-keeping — a distinctively Reformation-grace reading. |
| **vv. 38-42** | Reformed (R.C. Sproul) sees a "comparative" not a "contrast" — service is good, listening is better. Lutheran (1517.org) resists turning Mary and Martha into categories/archetypes and sees each sister as focused on one of the two great commandments, with finitude (not sin) as the core problem. Evangelical (bible.org) emphasizes Jesus' refusal to impose gender-role stereotypes — Mary is commended as a disciple/learner. Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey) reads both women as engaged in different "ministries" (*diakonia*). |
